thesis: C. V. Raman discovered that a tiny fraction of scattered light changes colour by trading energy with molecular vibrations, giving every substance a unique fingerprint. He won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics, and machine-learning models now read these fingerprints to identify substances.

story.title: A new colour in scattered light
story.text: In Calcutta, Raman and his student K. S. Krishnan shone filtered sunlight through pure liquids and saw faint light of a different colour in the scattered beam. The light had swapped energy with the molecules' vibrations. Raman won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics, the first Asian to win a science Nobel.

story.title: Shifts make a fingerprint
story.text: Most photons keep the laser's colour (Rayleigh scattering). About one in ten million gives some energy to a vibration and comes out redder (Stokes scattering). Plotting how far each photon shifted, in cm⁻¹, gives peaks at each molecule's own vibrations. A different laser moves the colours, but the shifts stay the same, so they identify the molecule.

story.title: Machine learning reads spectra
story.text: Real spectra are noisy and similar molecules look alike. Researchers train machine-learning models, including convolutional neural networks that treat a spectrum like a one-dimensional image, to identify bacteria, spot cancerous tissue, catch counterfeit medicines and find microplastics. The networks learn which peaks and patterns tell one substance from another.

hint: Switch the molecule and watch new peaks grow. Try a short exposure and the spectrum turns noisy. Change the laser colour: the nm values move but the cm⁻¹ shifts stay put.
